result:
**Answer: $\dfrac{1-p_0}{1-m}$**

The limit is governed by a one-big-jump heuristic. The tail $\mathbb{P}(X>x)$ is stretched-exponential with $b<1$, so it is subexponential. Reaching level $x$ is then almost always achieved by a single large displacement of one particle, with the rest of the tree staying $O(1)$, and two large displacements are negligible.

The model matters here. The problem states that the offspring number is independent of the step $X$, so I take $X$ to be the displacement attached to each individual's reproduction event, shared by its children. Under this reading, a large step causes a crossing only if the individual actually has at least one child. The relevant events therefore have probability $\mathbb{P}(Z\ge1,\ X>x)=(1-p_0)\,\mathbb{P}(X>x)$ per individual.

The expected number of individuals in generation $n$ is $m^n$, so the expected number of individuals that reproduce and carry a large step is

$$\sum_{n\ge 0} m^n (1-p_0)\,\mathbb{P}(X>x) = \frac{1-p_0}{1-m}\,\mathbb{P}(X>x).$$

Summing over generations gives $\mathbb{P}(M>x)\sim \frac{1-p_0}{1-m}\,\mathbb{P}(X>x)$, which yields the limit.

If instead each child received an independent displacement, the count would be $\sum_{n\ge1} m^n\,\mathbb{P}(X>x)=\frac{m}{1-m}\,\mathbb{P}(X>x)$. That version does not involve $p_0$, so the problem's phrasing points to the shared-step model.

I did not verify this against the source paper.

ANSWER: $\frac{1-p_0}{1-m}$
